1.meaning: By those who violently tear out and drag away — an oath sworn by the angels who pull out (the souls of the wicked) with force. The active participle names the doers as 'the ones who extract/wrench out.'

parts.en: feminine plural ending in the genitive case

1.grammar: An oath: 'wa' means 'I swear/By…'. 'al-' is 'the'. 'nāziʿ' is an active participle ('one who pulls out'); the long '-āt-' makes it feminine plural ('those who pull out'), used for the angels as a group. The final '-i' is the genitive ending required after the oath particle 'wa'. The pattern 'fāʿil' (nāziʿ) marks the ongoing doer of the action.
1.root: ن-ز-ع (n-z-ʿ) — to pull out, wrench away, remove

2.meaning: Drowning-deep, i.e. with a forceful, total wrenching — describing how violently the souls are torn out, as if plunged and dragged. Functions adverbially: 'extracting them with utmost force.'
2.grammar: A verbal noun (the act itself, 'a drowning/wrenching'). The '-an' (tanwīn fatḥa, accusative) makes it an absolute object / adverb that intensifies the verb's force — 'they pull out with a thorough wrenching.' It is not 'the' anything; the '-an' also signals it is indefinite ('a').
2.root: غ-ر-ق (gh-r-q) — to drown, sink, be submerged

1.meaning: And by those who gently loosen and draw out — an oath by the angels who untie and ease out (the souls of the righteous) softly. 'Those who unbind/draw out.'

parts.en: feminine plural ending in the genitive case

1.grammar: 'wa' here joins to the previous oath ('and by…'). In the Uthmanic mushaf the conjunctive wāw is written merged onto the following definite article, producing the geminated-looking وَّ (wa + al-nāshiṭāt); this is a scribal/orthographic convention, not a sign of any sound-change — it is NOT related to hamzat al-waṣl (which concerns elision of a glottal stop). 'al-' is 'the'. 'nāshiṭ' is an active participle ('one who draws out gently'), made feminine plural by '-āt-' for the angels. The final '-i' is genitive, matching the oath construction begun in verse 1.
1.root: ن-ش-ط (n-sh-ṭ) — to draw/pull out, untie a knot, do briskly

2.meaning: With a gentle drawing-out — describing the soft, easy manner in which the good souls are loosened free. Adverbial: 'drawing them out gently.'
2.grammar: A verbal noun ('a drawing-out'). The '-an' (accusative, tanwīn fatḥa) is an absolute object reinforcing the verb — 'they draw out with a real, gentle drawing.' The '-an' also marks it as indefinite ('a').
2.root: ن-ش-ط (n-sh-ṭ) — to draw/pull out, untie, act briskly

1.meaning: And by those who glide swimmingly — an oath by the angels who move smoothly and swiftly (as a swimmer glides through water). 'Those who swim/float along.'

parts.en: feminine plural ending in the genitive case

1.grammar: 'wa' joins to the running oath ('and by…'), written doubled in connection. 'al-' is 'the'. 'sābiḥ' is an active participle ('one who swims/glides'), made feminine plural by '-āt-' for the angels. The final '-i' is the genitive ending of the oath construction.
1.root: س-ب-ح (s-b-ḥ) — to swim, glide, float, move freely

2.meaning: With a gliding/swimming motion — describing the smooth, swift way they move. Adverbial: 'gliding along smoothly.'
2.grammar: A verbal noun ('a gliding/swimming'). The '-an' (accusative) is an absolute object intensifying the verb — 'they glide with a true glide.' The '-an' also marks indefiniteness ('a').
2.root: س-ب-ح (s-b-ḥ) — to swim, glide, float freely

1.meaning: Then by those who race ahead and outstrip — an oath by the angels who surge forward and take the lead. 'Those who get ahead / outrun.'

parts.en: then / and so (continuing the oath in sequence)
feminine plural ending in the genitive case

1.grammar: 'fa' means 'then/and so', adding sequence to the oath ('then by…'). 'al-' is 'the'. 'sābiq' is an active participle ('one who races ahead/outstrips'), feminine plural via '-āt-' for the angels. The final '-i' is the genitive ending of the continuing oath.
1.root: س-ب-ق (s-b-q) — to precede, outstrip, race ahead, win a race

2.meaning: With a racing/outstripping — describing how they vie and surge to the front. Adverbial: 'racing ahead in a true race.'
2.grammar: A verbal noun ('a racing'). The '-an' (accusative) is an absolute object reinforcing the verb — 'they race with a real racing.' The '-an' also marks it indefinite ('a').
2.root: س-ب-ق (s-b-q) — to precede, outstrip, race ahead

1.meaning: Then by those who manage and direct (the) affair — an oath by the angels who carry out and regulate the command (of Allah). 'Those who arrange/administer matters.'

parts.en: then / and so (continuing the oath in sequence)
feminine plural ending in the genitive case

1.grammar: 'fa' means 'then/and so' (oath in sequence). 'al-' is 'the'. The participle is 'mudabbir' — note the doubled bāʾ (shadda), so it is transliterated with two b's (mu-dab-bir), not 'mudabir'. It is a Form II active participle (pattern mufaʿʿil: the 'mu-' prefix, a kasra before the last root letter, and a geminated middle root letter), meaning 'one who manages/regulates'; the gemination conveys deliberate, organized handling. It is feminine plural via '-āt-' for the angels. The final '-i' is the genitive ending of the oath.
1.root: د-ب-ر (d-b-r) — back/end; to manage, arrange, direct the outcome of an affair

2.meaning: A matter / a command / an affair — here the divine command or business that the angels are charged with carrying out. It is the thing being managed.
2.grammar: A noun in the accusative ('-an', tanwīn fatḥa) functioning as the direct object of the participle 'mudabbirāt' — 'those who manage an affair.' The '-an' also marks it indefinite ('a matter/command'). Unlike the verbal nouns above, this is the actual object acted upon, not an adverb.
2.root: أ-م-ر (ʾ-m-r) — to command, order; matter, affair

1.meaning: (On) the Day — pointing to a specific future Day (the Day of Resurrection). It sets the time-frame: 'the Day when…'.

parts.en: accusative ending (adverb of time: 'on the Day')

1.grammar: A noun with the '-a' ending (fatḥa, accusative). Here the accusative works as an adverb of time — 'on the Day (when)…' — and 'yawma' is also in a construct with the verb that follows ('the Day [when] it quakes'), which is why it shows the bare '-a' vowel rather than tanwīn.

2.meaning: It quakes / trembles violently — the convulsive shaking of the earth (or of all things) at the Blast of resurrection. A present/future verb: 'will quake / is quaking.'
2.grammar: A present/future-tense verb. The 'ta-' prefix marks a third-person feminine singular subject ('it/she quakes') — matching the feminine 'the quaking one (Blast)' that follows. The final '-u' is the indicative ending, marking a plain ongoing/future action ('quakes / will quake'), not a command or a negated/subjunctive form.
2.root: ر-ج-ف (r-j-f) — to quake, shake violently, convulse, tremble

3.meaning: The one that violently shakes or convulses — a feminine active participle used as a name for the great Blast (the first blast of the Trumpet) that will make the earth and all creation quake on the Last Day.
3.grammar: A feminine active participle ('the shaking/quaking one') functioning as a noun. The 'al-' is 'the'; note the sun-letter 'r' doubles after it (l-rājifatu). The final '-u' ending is nominative, marking it as the subject — here the subject of the verb 'will come to pass' in the verse.
3.root: ر-ج-ف (r-j-f) — to quake, convulse, shake violently

1.meaning: It follows it / comes right after it — describing how a second event comes immediately on the heels of the first.
1.grammar: A present-tense verb, 3rd-person feminine singular ('she/it follows'); the 'ta-' prefix marks this 3rd-feminine subject (the second Blast). The final '-u' on the verb stem is the indicative mood, the plain stating form ('follows'). The attached '-hā' ('it') is the object — what is being followed, i.e. the first Blast.

2.meaning: The one that comes next, the follower-up — a feminine active participle naming the second Blast that follows immediately behind the first.
2.grammar: A feminine active participle ('the one that follows after') used as a noun. As with al-rājifa, 'al-' is 'the' and the sun-letter 'r' doubles after it (l-rādifatu). The final '-u' is nominative, marking it as the subject of its clause.
2.root: ر-د-ف (r-d-f) — to follow behind, come in succession (as a rider seated behind another)

1.meaning: Hearts — the inner seat of feeling, thought, and conviction; here the hearts of the deniers on the Day of Resurrection.
1.grammar: A plural noun ('hearts'). The ending '-un' does two things: the '-u' is nominative (this is the subject of the verse), and the final '-n' sound (nunation/tanwīn) marks it as indefinite — 'certain hearts' rather than 'the hearts'.
1.root: ق-ل-ب (q-l-b) — heart; to turn over, fluctuate

2.meaning: On that day — a fixed time-expression pointing to the Day of Resurrection; literally 'on a day, that one (the moment just mentioned)'.

parts.en: of that (a time-tag pointing to the mentioned moment, with '-in' ending)

2.grammar: A compound time-adverb, 'on that day'. 'Yawm' ('day') carries the '-a' ending that marks a time/place adverb ('when, on'). It is fused with '-idhin', a pointer meaning 'at that (already-mentioned) time'; the '-in' on it is a tanwīn standing in for the omitted clause ('the day when [the Blast comes]'). The 'y' is doubled here only because of the preceding word in recitation (the verse opens 'qulūbun yawma-idhin').

3.meaning: Throbbing, palpitating, beating violently with dread — a feminine active participle describing hearts pounding in terror.
3.grammar: A feminine active participle ('throbbing, palpitating'), serving as the predicate (description) of 'hearts' (qulūbun): 'hearts… [will be] throbbing'. The ending '-un' is nominative (agreeing with the subject 'hearts') plus nunation marking it indefinite. The leading 'w' is doubled only for recitation linking with the preceding 'yawma-idhin'.
3.root: و-ج-ف (w-j-f) — to throb, palpitate, beat fast

1.meaning: Their eyes — the eyes belonging to those terrified hearts/people; the organs of sight, here cast down in humiliation.
1.grammar: A plural noun ('eyes, sights') with an attached possessive pronoun '-hā' ('their/its'), referring back to the hearts/people. The noun's case ending is nominative '-u' (it is the subject of its clause), sitting just before the pronoun (abṣāru-hā); attaching the pronoun makes the phrase definite, so no nunation appears.
1.root: ب-ص-ر (b-ṣ-r) — sight, vision; to see, perceive

2.meaning: Humbled, downcast, lowered in awe and abasement — a feminine active participle describing eyes brought low before the overwhelming reality of the Day.
2.grammar: A feminine active participle ('humbled, downcast'), the predicate (description) of 'their eyes' (abṣāruhā): 'their eyes [will be] downcast'. The ending '-un' is nominative — agreeing with the subject 'eyes' — plus nunation marking it indefinite. The feminine singular form is used because 'eyes' is a non-human plural, which Arabic treats as grammatically feminine singular.
2.root: خ-ش-ع (kh-sh-ʿ) — humility, submissiveness, lowering oneself in awe

1.meaning: They say / they keep saying — used here of the deniers voicing their mocking objection.
1.grammar: A present-tense verb, 3rd-person masculine plural ('they say'). The 'ya-' prefix together with the '-ūna' ending marks the 'they (men)' subject. The full '-ūna' ending (with its final '-na' kept) is the indicative mood — the plain ongoing/stating form, 'they say / they keep saying'.

2.meaning: Is it really that we…? — an emphatic, incredulous question. It fuses the question-marker 'a-' ('is it that…?') with 'inna' (a particle of strong emphasis/certainty) and the pronoun 'we', producing the deniers' astonished, mocking 'Are we really…?'.

parts.en: indeed / truly (emphasis particle); its doubled nūn also absorbs the nūn of the following pronoun
we / us (pronoun نَا; its نَ merges into inna's shaddah, leaving only the alif written)

2.grammar: Not a single word but a fused cluster: interrogative 'a-' ('is it…?') + emphasizer 'inna' ('indeed') + the 1st-person-plural pronoun '-nā' ('we/us'). The surface form ءَاِنَّا is a contraction of ءَاِنَّنَا: the pronoun نَا still carries its own nūn, but that نَ assimilates into (idghām) and is represented by the geminate nūn (shaddah) of inna, so only the alif of نَا remains visible. Thus one half of the doubled nūn belongs to inna and the other stands for the absorbed نَ of نَا. 'Inna' has no direct English equivalent — it adds force and certainty ('Are we really, truly…?') and grammatically puts its following pronoun in the accusative; here that is '-nā' ('us'), the thing being questioned.

3.meaning: Surely going to be brought back / returned — describing the deniers' disbelief that they will be restored to life (or to their former state) after death.

parts.en: ones who are… (masculine plural, nominative ending)

3.grammar: A passive participle ('one who is brought back') in the masculine plural ('ones who are returned'). The prefix 'la-' is an emphasizer ('surely, indeed') that pairs with the earlier 'inna' to intensify the statement. The plural ending '-ūna' is nominative — it marks these as the predicate/subject-complement ('[that] we are surely the returned-ones').
3.root: ر-د-د (r-d-d) — to return, send back, restore

4.meaning: In / into — a preposition indicating being inside or placed within something; here 'returned into (our former state / our graves)'.
4.grammar: A preposition meaning 'in, into, within'. It is invariable — its form never changes for case or number. It governs the noun that follows it, putting that noun in the genitive (the 'of/with respect to' case), and links the action of being 'returned' to the place or state one is returned into.
4.root: — (preposition; no triliteral root)

5.meaning: The former condition or original state of life. The word names the state someone was in before death; here the disbelievers mockingly ask whether they will be 'returned to the ḥāfira,' i.e. brought back to their first state of living existence. The form literally evokes the 'dug-out' hollow (a hoof-print, or by extension the grave/the beginning), pointing to a return to the starting point.

parts.en: one that digs / the dug-out (former) state
genitive ending (governed by the preceding preposition 'fī')

5.grammar: A feminine singular noun of the active-participle pattern (fāʿila) with the definite article 'al-' ('the'). The final '-i' is the genitive case, governed by the preposition 'fī' ('in/to') that precedes it in the verse (fī l-ḥāfira, 'into the former state'). The 'tā marbūṭa' (-a/-at) is the feminine ending.
5.root: ح-ف-ر (ḥ-f-r) — to dig, hollow out (hence the 'first/original' state, like a dug-out beginning)

1.meaning: An exclamation of astonished denial introducing a time clause: roughly 'What! When...?' It combines a particle expressing shocked rejection with 'when', so the speakers are incredulously protesting: 'What — when we have become decayed bones — are we really to be brought back?' It frames the resurrection as something they find absurd.
1.grammar: Two indeclinable particles, so there is no case ending. The opening hamza 'a-' is the interrogative of denial and amazement. 'Idhā' is an adverb of future time ('when') that sets up a condition/circumstance; it does not change form.

2.meaning: 'We were / we had become.' It is the past (perfect) tense of the verb 'to be' (kāna) with 'we', used here to state a past or completed condition: 'when we were / had become...'. Kāna links a subject to a state, so the sense is 'we came to be (such-and-such).'
2.grammar: A past-tense (perfect) verb meaning 'we were / we had become.' The attached '-nā' ending means the subject is 'we'. The hollow root's middle 'wāw' drops in this form, giving 'kun-' before the '-nā'. There is no case ending on a verb; tense is past and the doer is first-person plural ('we').
2.root: ك-و-ن (k-w-n) — to be, to exist, to become

3.meaning: Bones. The plural of 'ʿaẓm' (a bone), denoting the skeletal remains. In context it is what the dead body has been reduced to: mere bones.
3.grammar: A masculine broken (irregular) plural noun, indefinite. The '-an' ending (with tanwīn/nunation) marks the accusative case: it is the predicate of 'kunnā' ('we were bones'), i.e. what 'we became'. The 'an' tells you the noun is both indefinite ('bones', not 'the bones') and in the accusative.

4.meaning: Decayed, crumbling, rotten — describing bones so old they have become brittle and hollow, the kind that crumble or make a sound when wind passes through them. It stresses utter disintegration, deepening the disbelievers' point that such remains could never live again.
4.grammar: A feminine adjective on the 'faʿil' pattern, describing 'ʿiẓāman' ('bones'). It matches that noun in being indefinite and accusative, shown by the '-an' (tanwīn) ending. The feminine 'tā' (-at) agrees with the (grammatically feminine) plural 'bones'. So: 'decayed bones'.
4.root: ن-خ-ر (n-kh-r) — to be rotten/hollow; (of bones) to decay and crumble

1.meaning: 'They said.' Past tense of 'to say' with a masculine plural subject ('they'). It reports the disbelievers' speech that follows.
1.grammar: A past-tense (perfect) verb. The '-ū' ending means the subject is 'they' (masculine plural). The final silent 'alif' (وا) is just a spelling convention after the plural '-ū' and is not pronounced. Being a verb, it has no case ending; tense is past, doer is third-person plural.

2.meaning: 'That' — a demonstrative pointing to something regarded as far off (here, the return/resurrection just mentioned). Often rendered 'that' (and sometimes 'this'); it singles out the previously named thing: 'that [return]...'.

parts.en: particle of distance / addressing the listener ('there/you')

2.grammar: A feminine singular demonstrative pronoun ('that one'). It is indeclinable, so it takes no case ending. The '-ka' element signals distance (something far) and is addressed to the listener. It refers to the feminine noun 'karra' ('return') coming up: 'that return'.

3.meaning: 'In that case / then.' A response particle meaning that what is said is a consequence of what was just mentioned: 'If we really are brought back — then that return is a loss!' It marks the statement as an answer to, and result of, the preceding idea.

parts.en: in that case / then (particle of consequence)

3.grammar: An indeclinable response/consequence particle; it has no case ending. The final '-an' (with tanwīn) is an intrinsic part of the word, not a case marker. It signals that the following statement is the result of the situation just supposed.

4.meaning: A single return; one more turn or repetition — specifically being brought back to life once again after death. The pattern (faʿla) denotes one instance of an act, so it is literally 'one return.'

parts.en: a returning / a turning back (single instance)

4.grammar: A feminine singular noun of the single-instance pattern (faʿla), indefinite. The '-un' (tanwīn) ending marks the nominative case: it is the subject described by the demonstrative and the adjective — 'that [would be] a return [that is] losing.' The 'an'/'un' nunation also shows it is indefinite ('a return').
4.root: ك-ر-ر (k-r-r) — to return, repeat, turn back again

5.meaning: Loss-bringing; doomed to loss. An active participle describing the 'return' as one that ends in ruin for them — a losing, failed venture. They sarcastically say that if resurrection is real, then coming back would only spell their loss.
5.grammar: A feminine active participle (fāʿila pattern) describing 'karra' ('return'). It agrees with that noun: feminine, indefinite, and nominative, shown by the '-un' (tanwīn) ending. So it is an adjective: 'a losing return' / 'a return that brings loss'.
5.root: خ-س-ر (kh-s-r) — to lose, suffer loss, come to ruin

1.meaning: 'Then it is only / but it is merely...' It joins two parts: 'fa-' ('then/so', linking to what precedes) and 'innamā' ('it is only / nothing but'), a restrictive emphasis that limits the matter to a single thing. Together they stress that all it takes is just one thing (one mighty blast).
1.grammar: A cluster of particles, indeclinable, so no case endings. 'Fa-' connects this verse to the previous and can carry the sense 'then'. 'Inna' is a strong assertion ('indeed'), and the attached 'mā' turns it into 'innamā' = 'only / merely', restricting the statement to one thing. The combination cancels 'inna's' usual case effect.

2.meaning: 'It / she' — a standalone subject pronoun for a single feminine (or grammatically feminine) thing. Here it refers ahead to the feminine noun for the great Blast/Cry: 'it is but a single shout.'
2.grammar: An independent (standalone) subject pronoun, third-person feminine singular. It is indeclinable and takes no case ending. It functions as the subject of the sentence ('it is only...'), pointing to a feminine noun — the single mighty Blast named in the next verse.

3.meaning: A single cry, shout, or blast — specifically a violent rebuke or driving-shout. Here it denotes the one mighty Blast of the Trumpet that suffices to raise the dead. The feminine ending often marks a single instance of the act (one shout, given once).
3.grammar: A feminine singular noun. The tā' marbūṭa (-a-t-) makes it feminine and here marks a single occurrence ('one shout'). The final '-un' (tanwīn ḍamma) is the nominative/subject case and signals it is indefinite ('a shout'); it is the doer of the verb in 'it will be only one shout'.
3.root: ز-ج-ر (z-j-r) — to drive away by shouting, to rebuke harshly

4.meaning: One, single, sole — emphasizing that just one Blast is enough; no second is needed.

parts.en: and (its wāw doubled onto the word's own first wāw)
one / single (the word minus its initial wāw, which merged with the conjunction)

4.grammar: A feminine singular adjective describing 'zajratun' (the shout), so it too is feminine to agree with it. The tā' marbūṭa marks the feminine. The final '-un' (tanwīn ḍamma) is the nominative/subject case and marks it indefinite — matching the noun it describes ('a single shout'). The whole spoken form 'wwāḥidatun' is the conjunction wa- ('and/but') fused onto the adjective 'wāḥida': the conjunction's wāw and the adjective's own initial wāw merge into one doubled w- (shown here as وَّ), so the remaining segment written with alif reads '-āḥida'.
4.root: و-ح-د (w-ḥ-d) — to be one, single, alone; oneness

1.meaning: And then, all of a sudden — combining 'and' with a word of surprise that signals something happening abruptly and unexpectedly ('and behold, at once...').
1.grammar: Two particles, so there is no case-ending to mark. 'fa-' is a connector meaning 'and then / so', showing what follows comes next in sequence. 'idhā' here is the 'idhā of surprise' (idhā al-fujā'iyya): it dramatizes a sudden, unexpected scene — 'and all at once, there they are...'.

2.meaning: They / them — a standalone pronoun referring to the people who were dead and are now suddenly raised. As a freestanding word it can add emphasis ('they themselves').
2.grammar: A detached (standalone) personal pronoun, third person masculine plural, 'they'. Such pronouns do not change for case; the fixed '-um' ending simply marks 'they/them' (men, or a mixed group). Here it is the subject of the sudden scene: 'and at once, there they are, on the surface.'

3.meaning: On the surface of the earth — 'al-sāhira' is a name for the open, level face of the ground (the plain on which all are gathered for Judgment). The word literally evokes wakefulness, as if the bare earth never sleeps. The phrase says the resurrected are suddenly standing upon it.

parts.en: the (wakeful) open surface of the earth

3.grammar: A preposition 'bi-' ('on/upon') joined to a feminine noun carrying 'al-' ('the'). The tā' marbūṭa marks the feminine. The final '-i' (kasra) is the genitive ending, required because the noun follows the preposition 'bi-'; the whole phrase functions as 'upon the surface'. (The form 'sāhira' is an active participle pattern of 's-h-r', literally 'the one awake/wakeful'.)
3.root: س-ه-ر (s-h-r) — to stay awake, be wakeful at night

1.meaning: A question-word that turns a statement into a yes/no question ('has...?', 'is it that...?'). Here it gently introduces the question and can carry a sense of inviting attention: 'Has there indeed come to you...?'
1.grammar: An interrogative particle, so it has no case-ending. It is placed at the head of a sentence to make it a yes/no question. It often implies that an affirmative answer is expected or is about to be given.

2.meaning: It came to you / has reached you — the act of a piece of news or a story arriving at a person. With the attached 'you', it means 'it has come to you'.
2.grammar: A past-tense verb, third person masculine singular ('he/it came'), agreeing with its subject 'the story' (which comes after it). The verb ends in a long '-ā' (written with alif maqṣūra, ٰى) because its final root-letter is a weak letter. The attached '-ka' is the object pronoun 'you' (one male, addressing the Prophet ﷺ): 'it came to you.'

3.meaning: An account, narration, or report — a story or piece of news that is told. In the Qur'an it frequently introduces a meaningful narrative drawn from the past.
3.grammar: A masculine singular noun and the subject of the verb 'atā' ('came'). The final '-u' (ḍamma) is the nominative/subject case, marking it as the doer ('the story came to you'). It has no tanwīn (no '-un') because it is the first term of a possessive pair, joined to the following name: 'the story OF Moses'.
3.root: ح-د-ث (ḥ-d-th) — to happen anew, to relate/narrate; news, speech

4.meaning: Mūsā — the Prophet Moses (peace be upon him). A proper name borrowed into Arabic; it does not derive from an Arabic root.
4.grammar: A proper name, here in the possessive (genitive) position — 'the story OF Mūsā'. Because it is a foreign/indeclinable name ending in a fixed long '-ā' (written with alif maqṣūra, ٰى), its ending never changes for case; the long '-ā' stays the same whatever its role in the sentence.
4.root: — (proper name; no triliteral root)

1.meaning: When / at the time when — points back to a specific past moment to begin recounting it ('when...', 'the time his Lord called him').
1.grammar: A time-word (adverb/particle) referring to a definite moment in the past, so it carries no changing case-ending. It introduces the scene that follows: 'when his Lord called him...'. It is typically attached to the story being told as 'recall the time when...'.

2.meaning: He called him / called out to him — the act of summoning or calling someone, here Allah calling Moses. With the attached 'him' it means 'He called him'.
2.grammar: A past-tense verb, third person masculine singular ('he called'), from a pattern (Form III) that often means calling out to someone. It ends in a long '-ā' (written with alif maqṣūra, ٰى) because its final root-letter is weak. The attached '-hu' is the object pronoun 'him' (Moses): 'He called him.' The doer 'his Lord' comes right after.
2.root: ن-د-ي / ن-د-و (n-d-y) — to call, call out, summon

3.meaning: His Lord — 'Rabb' is the Master and Sustainer who creates, owns, nurtures, and governs all that He has made; here it refers to Allah. With 'his' attached, it means 'his Lord', i.e., Moses's Lord.
3.grammar: A masculine singular noun with an attached possessive pronoun 'his'. The '-u' (ḍamma) on 'rabb-' is the nominative/subject case, marking it as the doer of 'called' ('his Lord called him'). The attached '-hu' ('his') makes it definite and links it to Moses. The long pronunciation 'rabbuhū' is the normal way this 'his' is recited after a '-u' vowel.
3.root: ر-ب-ب (r-b-b) — to nurture, sustain, master; lordship and care

4.meaning: In the valley. A 'wādī' is a low-lying watercourse or valley between hills or mountains — here referring to the specific sacred valley where Allah spoke to Moses.
4.grammar: The prefix 'bi-' means 'in/at' and always forces what follows into the genitive (the 'of/with' case). 'al-' is 'the'. The noun normally ends in a final long 'ī' (al-wādī), but here it is written without that final letter and pronounced 'wādi' — a recognized Qur'anic spelling of this defective/weak-final noun. The genitive case (governed by 'bi-') is what marks it as the object of 'in'.
4.root: و-د-ي (w-d-y) — to flow; hence wādī, a valley/watercourse where water runs

5.meaning: The sanctified / made-holy. A passive description meaning something that has been purified and set apart as sacred — here describing the valley as consecrated holy ground.
5.grammar: This is a passive participle ('the one that has been sanctified') built on Form II, whose doubled middle letter (the shadda on the 'd') gives the sense of intensively making something holy. The final '-i' ending is genitive: it agrees with and describes the preceding genitive noun 'al-wādī' ('the valley'), so both share the same case — 'in the SACRED valley'.

6.meaning: Ṭuwā — the proper name of the sacred valley near Mount Sinai where Allah addressed Moses.

parts.en: ending: compensatory nunation (-an) replacing a dropped alif

6.grammar: A proper noun (place name) standing in apposition (badal / ʿaṭf bayān) to the preceding phrase 'al-wādī al-muqaddas' ('the sacred valley') — it renames the same place, so it takes that phrase's GENITIVE case, not the accusative. It is written with final 'alif maqṣūra' (ى) bearing tanwīn pronounced '-an', but this is tanwīn ʿiwaḍ (compensatory nunation): the nūn-sound substitutes for a dropped final alif of the weak-final noun and is NOT a case-marking ending. As a name it identifies the location; its grammatical case is genitive by apposition while the visible '-an' merely compensates for the missing letter.

1.meaning: Go! A direct command telling someone to set out and depart toward a destination.
1.grammar: A singular masculine command (imperative) addressed to one person: 'Go!' The initial 'i-' is a helper-vowel added only because the root's first letter carries no vowel of its own and Arabic cannot begin a word on a silent consonant. The bare, voweless final ('-hab', no case ending) is exactly how the command form is marked — it is clipped because an order needs no further inflection.

2.meaning: To / toward. A preposition expressing motion or direction up to a goal or endpoint.
2.grammar: An indeclinable preposition meaning 'to/toward'; written with a final long 'ā' (alif maqṣūra). It does not change its form, but it governs the following noun into the genitive case (here 'Firʿawn' → 'Firʿawna'). It marks the endpoint of the motion in 'Go to…'.

3.meaning: Pharaoh — the title/name of the king of Egypt to whom Moses was sent.
3.grammar: A proper name. It is a 'diptote' — a noun that refuses normal nunation and takes only two endings — so in the genitive (required here after the preposition 'ilā', 'to') it shows '-a' rather than the usual '-i'. So although it is the object of 'to', its case-vowel is the special diptote '-a'. The '-a' here therefore signals 'to Pharaoh'.
3.root: — (proper name, of Egyptian origin; no Arabic root)

4.meaning: Indeed he… 'Inna' is an emphasis particle that strongly affirms the statement ('truly, certainly'), and the attached 'he' is its subject. Together: 'Truly he…'.
4.grammar: 'Inna' is an emphatic particle that opens a sentence to assert it forcefully; it grammatically takes a following noun or pronoun into the accusative as its subject. The attached pronoun '-hu' ('he') is that subject — written with a long 'ū' (innahū) in full recitation. There is no case ending to explain on a fixed pronoun; its role is simply 'he', emphasized by 'inna': 'Indeed he…'.
4.root: — (particle + pronoun; no root)

5.meaning: He has transgressed — he overstepped all proper limits, rebelled, and became tyrannically excessive (against Allah and against people).
5.grammar: A past-tense verb, third-person masculine singular: 'he transgressed/rebelled'. The root's final weak letter surfaces as a long 'ā' (written as alif maqṣūra, ṭaghā), which here carries the built-in 'he (did)' meaning of the past tense. It is the predicate of 'inna' from the previous word: 'Indeed he HAS transgressed.'
5.root: ط-غ-ي (ṭ-gh-y) — to exceed all bounds, overflow, rebel, tyrannize

1.meaning: And/then say! A command to speak or utter the words that follow, joined to what came before.
1.grammar: The prefix 'fa-' is a connector meaning 'and so/then', linking this order to the previous command and showing it follows in sequence. 'Qul' is a singular masculine imperative, 'Say!' Its final consonant is voweless ('-qul', no case ending), which is precisely how a command is formed — clipped, needing no further inflection.

2.meaning: A question-word that turns a statement into a yes/no question ('has...?', 'is it that...?'). Here it gently introduces the question and can carry a sense of inviting attention: 'Has there indeed come to you...?'
2.grammar: An interrogative particle, so it has no case-ending. It is placed at the head of a sentence to make it a yes/no question. It often implies that an affirmative answer is expected or is about to be given.

3.meaning: For you / to you. A preposition 'for/to' with an attached 'you', expressing that something pertains to or is offered to the addressee.
3.grammar: The preposition 'li-' ('for/to'), which here shifts to 'la-' before an attached pronoun. The suffix '-ka' is 'you' (one male). Attached pronouns after a preposition are in the genitive, but their form is fixed, so '-ka' simply means 'you'; the whole means 'for you' — i.e., 'is there [a path] FOR YOU to purify yourself?'

4.meaning: To / toward. The same preposition 'ilā' ('to'), here introducing the goal/aim — 'toward [purifying yourself]'.
4.grammar: An indeclinable preposition meaning 'to/toward', written with final long 'ā'. (The wavy madda mark over it here reflects the recitation lengthening that occurs because the next word begins with a hamza.) It governs what follows into the genitive and points to the goal: '[the way] to that you purify yourself'.
4.root: — (particle/preposition; no root)

5.meaning: That / to. 'An' is a subordinating particle that turns the following verb into a 'to do' phrase — roughly English 'to…' or 'that [one should]…'.
5.grammar: A particle that introduces a following present-tense verb and puts it into the subjunctive (the 'in order to / that one should' mood), turning the verb into a noun-like idea ('the purifying of yourself'). Combined with the preceding 'ilā', it yields 'toward THAT you purify yourself' = 'to purify yourself'. It is a fixed particle with no ending of its own.

6.meaning: To purify yourself — to cleanse your soul of disbelief and sin and grow in righteousness. The verb carries the sense of inner moral growth, not mere ritual washing: to develop into someone spiritually pure.
6.grammar: A present-tense verb, 2nd person masculine singular ('you'). The ta- prefix marks the 'you' subject. The doubled middle letter (zakka-) makes it an intensive 'Form V' reflexive verb meaning to purify one's own self. The final long -ā is the verb's weak ending (the root's last letter, originally a 'y/w', appears as ā here); after the preceding particle 'an' ('that/would you'), it reads as a subjunctive — 'that you purify yourself.'

1.meaning: And I will guide you — 'and that I should lead you' onto the right path. The speaker (Moses) offers to direct Pharaoh toward knowledge of his Lord.
1.grammar: A present-tense verb, 1st person singular ('I'), with the prefix a- marking the 'I' subject and the attached -ka meaning 'you' as its object. The final -a on the verb (ahdiy-a) is a subjunctive ending ('that I may guide'), produced by the implied particle 'an' carried over from the previous line; it is not a past-tense or indicative form. The wa- simply joins this to the preceding clause.

2.meaning: To / toward. A preposition expressing motion or direction up to a goal or endpoint.
2.grammar: An indeclinable preposition meaning 'to/toward'; written with a final long 'ā' (alif maqṣūra). It does not change its form, but it governs the following noun into the genitive case (here 'Firʿawn' → 'Firʿawna'). It marks the endpoint of the motion in 'Go to…'.

3.meaning: Your Lord — your Master, Owner, Sustainer and Caretaker. 'Rabb' means far more than a chief: the One who creates, owns, nurtures and brings each thing to its completion; here joined to 'your' (Pharaoh's true Lord).
3.grammar: A noun with the attached pronoun -ka ('your'). The -i vowel before the pronoun is the genitive (possessive) ending: it shows the word is governed by the preceding preposition 'ilā' ('to your Lord') and is possessed by 'you' — literally 'Lord of you.' The -ka is the possessor, 'your.'

4.meaning: So that you would then stand in awe — that you would come to fear Allah with a reverent, humbled dread born of knowing Him. 'Khashya' is fear mixed with awe and reverence, not mere fright.
4.grammar: A present-tense verb, 2nd person masculine singular ('you'), with the ta- prefix marking the 'you' subject. The connector fa- means 'so/and then,' showing this fear as the intended outcome of being guided. The final long -ā is the verb's weak root-ending (the final 'y' surfaces as ā); after fa- expressing purpose it carries a subjunctive sense — 'so that you would stand in awe.'
4.root: خ-ش-ي (kh-sh-y) — reverent fear, awe before something great

1.meaning: Then he showed him — 'so he caused him to see' it. Moses made Pharaoh witness the sign with his own eyes.
1.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd person masculine singular ('he'), with the attached -hu meaning 'him' as its object. This is the causative 'Form IV' of 'to see' — hence 'made him see / showed him.' There is no subject suffix because the bare past-tense stem already means 'he.' The connector fa- means 'then/so,' marking the next event. The long -ā within arā-hu is the verb's weak root-ending (final 'y' surfacing as ā).

2.meaning: The sign — the miraculous proof, the God-given token meant to point beyond itself to Allah's truth and power. An 'āya' is a sign that signifies and demonstrates.
2.grammar: A definite singular feminine noun, 'the sign,' marked by the prefix al- ('the'). The final -a is the accusative ending, showing it is the direct object of 'showed' — the thing that was shown. (The feminine ending here is the 'open' ta, pronounced -ta because the next word follows.)
2.root: أ-ي-ي / أ-و-ي (ʾ-y-y) — sign, mark, token that points to something

3.meaning: The greatest — the supreme, most enormous one. Here it describes the sign as the 'great(est)' sign, the most overwhelming of the miracles given to Moses.
3.grammar: A definite feminine adjective, 'the greatest,' marked by al- ('the'). It is the feminine 'elative' form (the 'biggest/greatest' pattern) agreeing with the feminine noun 'sign.' Its case ending does not change in pronunciation because it ends in the fixed long -ā; in role it is accusative, matching 'the sign' it describes ('the greatest sign').

1.meaning: But he denied / rejected it as a lie — Pharaoh 'cried lies' against the sign and the message, treating the truth as false. The intensive verb stresses a flat, emphatic rejection.

parts.en: denied / declared to be a lie (intensive)

1.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd person masculine singular ('he'). The doubled middle letter (kadhdh-) makes it an intensive 'Form II' verb: not just 'he lied' but 'he branded (it) a lie / vehemently denied (it).' The final -a is the normal past-tense ending of the bare 'he' form. The connector fa- means 'then/but,' marking what Pharaoh did in response.
1.root: ك-ذ-ب (k-dh-b) — lying, falsehood (Form II: to call something a lie)

2.meaning: And he disobeyed — he rebelled against and defied the command of Allah, refusing to submit.
2.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd person masculine singular ('he'). There is no subject suffix because the bare past stem already means 'he.' The final long -ā is the verb's weak root-ending (the final 'y/w' surfaces as ā). The wa- simply joins it to the previous verb — 'denied and disobeyed.'

1.meaning: Then / thereafter — a connector that links what follows to what came before, but with a sense of sequence and some interval ('and then, after that'). Unlike a plain 'and,' it marks a later, further step.
1.grammar: An indeclinable connecting particle — it has no case, tense, or person ending and never changes form. It joins clauses while signaling order and delay: the next action came afterward, as a subsequent stage.

2.meaning: He turned his back — he went away, turning aside from the truth and the messenger; an emphatic 'he showed his back' and walked off in rejection.

parts.en: he turned his back / went away

2.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd person masculine singular ('he'). It is a 'Form IV' verb built on the root for 'back,' meaning 'to turn one's back / retreat.' There is no subject suffix because the bare past stem already means 'he.' The final -a is the standard past-tense ending of the 'he' form.
2.root: د-ب-ر (d-b-r) — back, rear; turning away, retreating

3.meaning: Striving / hastening — he went about working hard and moving briskly, here exerting effort against the truth (scheming and rallying opposition).
3.grammar: A present-tense verb, 3rd person masculine singular ('he'), with the ya- prefix marking the 'he' subject. Set beside the past verbs around it, this ongoing present form paints the action as a vivid, continuing scene — 'turned his back, busily striving.' The final long -ā is the verb's weak root-ending (the final 'y' surfacing as ā).
3.root: س-ع-ي (s-ʿ-y) — to strive, run, hasten, exert effort

1.meaning: And he gathered/assembled (people together in one place). The verb describes mustering or rounding up a group, here Pharaoh assembling his people and magicians.
1.grammar: The prefix fa- means 'then' or 'and so', linking this action in sequence to what came before. The verb is past tense, third-person masculine singular ('he did'); the final -a is the normal ending of such a past-tense verb. Subject is 'he' (Pharaoh).

2.meaning: And he called out / proclaimed aloud. The verb means to summon or announce with a raised voice, here Pharaoh publicly proclaiming his false claim.
2.grammar: The prefix fa- means 'then/and so'. The verb is past tense, third-person masculine singular ('he called out'). It comes from a 'weak' root ending in a vowel, so instead of a short -a it ends in a long -ā (written with a final alif/yā), which is the regular past-tense form for this type of verb.

1.meaning: Then he said / he declared. A straightforward verb of speech introducing the words that follow.
1.grammar: The prefix fa- means 'then/and so', continuing the sequence. The verb is past tense, third-person masculine singular ('he said'). The long -ā in the middle reflects a hollow root whose middle letter is a vowel; the verb ends in the regular past-tense -a.

2.meaning: 'I' — the standalone, emphatic first-person pronoun. Standing on its own (rather than as an attached ending), it emphatically asserts the speaker: 'I myself.' Here Pharaoh says 'I am...'
2.grammar: This is an independent personal pronoun meaning 'I'. Pronouns like this do not take case endings or change form. Used as the subject of a nominal (verb-less) sentence, it stands for 'I am...', with the predicate ('your lord') supplied by the next words.

3.meaning: Your Lord/Master — the One who owns, sustains, nurtures, and has full authority over you. 'Rabb' carries the linked senses of owner, sustainer, and the one who brings up and cares for; 'kum' makes it 'of you (all)'. Here it is Pharaoh's blasphemous self-claim.
3.grammar: A noun ('lord') with the attached pronoun 'kum' ('your', addressing more than one person), giving 'your Lord'. The -u on rabbu is the nominative ending, marking it as the predicate of 'I am' (the thing being asserted: 'I am your lord'). The pronoun's vowel appears as -kumu (rather than -kum) to ease pronunciation before the next word beginning with 'al-'.

4.meaning: The Most High / the Highest. A superlative describing supreme elevation and loftiness. As a divine attribute it belongs truly to Allah alone; on Pharaoh's lips it is an arrogant usurpation.
4.grammar: The prefix al- is the definite article 'the'. The word is a superlative ('most high'), built on the pattern for 'most/-est'. It comes from a weak root ending in a vowel, so it ends in a long -ā; this ending does not change for case. It functions as an adjective describing 'your lord' ('the most high').
4.root: ع-ل-و (ʿ-l-w) — height, loftiness, elevation

1.meaning: So He seized/overtook him — gripped and struck him with sudden, overpowering force. The verb implies a forceful, decisive taking hold; 'hu' = 'him' (Pharaoh).
1.grammar: The prefix fa- here means 'so/then', signalling the consequence ('so He seized him'). The verb is past tense, third-person masculine singular ('He seized'); its regular past-tense ending is -a. The attached 'hu' ('him') is the object — the one seized. The subject 'Allah' is named in the next word.

2.meaning: Allah — the proper name of the One True God, the sole and supreme Deity. It is a unique name, not a common noun, and has no plural or feminine.
2.grammar: The proper name of Allah. The final -u is the nominative ending, marking 'Allah' as the subject/doer of the preceding verb — i.e. it is Allah who 'seized him'.

3.meaning: An exemplary punishment — a punishment so severe it serves as a warning deterrent to others, 'making an example' of the one punished.
3.grammar: A noun meaning 'a punishment that serves as a warning'. The final -a is the accusative ending: here it marks the punishment as the thing inflicted — the 'what' of the seizing ('He seized him as/with an exemplary punishment').

4.meaning: The last/latter — i.e. the Hereafter, the world to come. Literally 'the later (life)', the standard term for the next life as opposed to this present one.
4.grammar: The prefix al- is 'the'. The word is a feminine adjective/noun, 'the latter (life)', standing for the Hereafter. The final -i is the genitive ending, here meaning 'of' — 'an example of the next life' (a punishment relating to the Hereafter). The -t- is the feminine ending that appears when a suffix follows.
4.root: ء-خ-ر (ʾ-kh-r) — being last, coming after, the end

5.meaning: And the first/former — i.e. this present life, the world we live in now. Literally 'the earlier (life)', paired with 'the latter' to mean 'this life and the next'.
5.grammar: The prefix wa- means 'and'; al- (here 'l-' after the joining) is 'the'. The word is a feminine 'first/former (life)', the counterpart to 'the latter'. It comes from a defective root ending in a weak letter and so ends in a fixed long -ā that does not change for case; in sense it is linked to the preceding genitive ('of the latter and the first' = punishment touching both the next life and this one).
5.root: و-ل-ي (w-l-y) — being near/next, coming first, precedence

1.meaning: 'Indeed / surely' — an emphasis particle placed at the start of a sentence to affirm and strengthen what follows ('Truly, it is the case that...'). It adds certainty and weight rather than a translatable word of its own.
1.grammar: An emphasizing particle meaning 'indeed/surely'. It introduces a nominal sentence and grammatically puts the following noun (its subject) into the accusative case. It does not itself inflect; its role is to assert the statement emphatically ('Surely in this is a lesson...').

2.meaning: In / into — a preposition indicating being inside or placed within something; here 'returned into (our former state / our graves)'.
2.grammar: A preposition meaning 'in, into, within'. It is invariable — its form never changes for case or number. It governs the noun that follows it, putting that noun in the genitive (the 'of/with respect to' case), and links the action of being 'returned' to the place or state one is returned into.

3.meaning: A demonstrative pointing word meaning 'that' — referring to something distant or already mentioned. Here it points back to the preceding account of Pharaoh's fate, signalling 'that whole affair / that event'.
3.grammar: A masculine singular demonstrative for something far off, 'that (one) over there'. It is built from a pointing base (dhā) plus -li- (marking distance) plus -ka (addressing a single male listener). It is frozen in form — it does not take case endings — and here, governed by the preceding preposition fī, it serves as the topic: 'in that [there is]…'.

4.meaning: An admonitory lesson — a warning example one learns from by reflecting on it; literally a 'crossing over' from the visible event to the moral truth behind it. The la- prefix adds emphasis: 'truly a lesson'.
4.grammar: A feminine singular noun carrying the emphatic la- ('surely'). It is the khabar (predicate) of the opening 'inna ('Indeed in this there is…'), and the khabar of 'inna is put in the accusative — that is why it ends in -an (tanwīn fatḥ), the accusative with indefinite 'a/an'. So the ending marks it as the thing 'inna affirms to exist: 'Surely in this there is a lesson'.
4.root: ع-ب-ر (ʿ-b-r) — to cross over, pass through; hence to draw a lesson

5.meaning: A combination meaning 'for the one who' / 'for whoever' — joining the preposition 'for' to a relative pronoun that introduces an unnamed person: 'for anyone who…'.
5.grammar: The preposition li- ('for') attached to man ('whoever'), a relative pronoun used for persons. Both pieces are indeclinable — they never change their endings. The shadda written on this lām is a tajwīd (recitation) effect, not part of the word's spelling: the tanwīn (-an) ending the previous word ʿibratan merges into the lām (idghām of nūn into lām), so it is pronounced ʿibratal-liman. The phrase tells us who benefits from the lesson: the God-fearing person.

6.meaning: To stand in reverent awe and fear — specifically the fear born of knowing Allah's greatness, a fear mixed with reverence rather than mere dread. Here: 'whoever fears / holds Allah in awe'.
6.grammar: A present-tense verb, 'he fears'. The ya- prefix marks a third-person masculine singular subject ('he'). Because the root ends in a weak letter, the verb finishes in a long -ā (a 'defective' verb); in this position it stays in its plain (indicative) form, expressing an ongoing, habitual fearing. (The mark after it is a recitation pause sign, not part of the word.)
6.root: خ-ش-ي (kh-sh-y) — to fear with awe and reverence

1.meaning: An interrogative 'are you…?' — the question particle joined to the plural pronoun 'you', opening a rhetorical challenge: 'Is it you [who are harder to create]…?'
1.grammar: The question particle a- ('?') prefixed to antum, the detached pronoun 'you all' (masculine plural). The pronoun is fixed in form and serves as the subject of the comparison. Placing 'you' first throws emphasis on it: 'Is it you who are the harder creation…?' It addresses a group, hence the plural -tum.

2.meaning: More intense / harder / stronger — the comparative 'more ___' formed from 'severe, intense'. In context: 'more difficult [to create]'.
2.grammar: A comparative adjective ('more intense'), built on the pattern afʿal that means 'more ___'. The final -u is the nominative ending, because it is the predicate describing the subject ('you'): 'you are harder [to create]'. Comparatives of this shape stay invariable for gender and number. The doubled -dd- comes from the root's repeated letter.
2.root: ش-د-د (sh-d-d) — to be severe, intense, hard, strong

3.meaning: The act or aspect of creating / being created — 'in respect of creation'. It specifies in what way one thing is 'harder' than another: harder as regards its making.
3.grammar: A masculine verbal noun, 'creation'. The final -an (tanwīn fatḥ) is the accusative, here functioning as a 'specifier' (tamyīz): it pins down the respect in which the comparison holds — 'harder in regard to creation'. So the ending answers 'harder in what sense?' → 'in its creating'.

4.meaning: A connective 'or' that links the two sides of a question — 'or [is it]…?'. It pairs with the earlier 'is it…?' to weigh two alternatives: you, or the sky?
4.grammar: The particle am, 'or', used to join the second option in a direct question ('A… or B?'). Its base form is am; the final vowel here is -i, a helping vowel added only to ease pronunciation before the article 'al-' that follows (am + al-samāʾ → ami s-samāʾ). The -i carries no grammatical case meaning — it is purely for smooth linking.
4.root: — (connective particle, no triliteral root)

5.meaning: The sky / the heaven — the vast canopy raised above the earth; in this verse the second term of the comparison: '…or the sky [which He built]'.
5.grammar: A feminine noun, 'the sky', with the definite article al- ('the'). The final -u is the nominative ending, marking it as a subject — here the second item being compared ('or [is] the sky harder?'). The s of al- is doubled in pronunciation because s is a 'sun letter' that absorbs the l of the article. (The mark after it is a pause sign for recitation.)
5.root: س-م-و (s-m-w) — to be high, lofty; that which is above

6.meaning: He built it / constructed it — Allah erected and put together the heaven. The attached 'it' refers back to the sky.
6.grammar: A past-tense verb, 'he built', with no prefix — the bare past form already means 'he' did it (third-person masculine singular), the subject being Allah. The root ends in a weak letter, so the verb closes in long -ā. The suffix -hā is an attached object pronoun, 'it' (grammatically feminine, matching 'the sky'): 'He built it'.

1.meaning: He raised / lifted up high — Allah elevated the heaven's expanse. A plain statement of His act of raising it aloft.
1.grammar: A past-tense verb, 'he raised'. With no prefix and the final -a, it is the basic past form for a third-person masculine singular subject ('he'), namely Allah. The three open 'a' vowels (rafaʿa) are the standard sound-pattern of a simple past-tense verb. It takes the following word as its object: 'He raised its ceiling'.

2.meaning: Its ceiling / its roof — the height or vault of the heaven; the 'roof' of the sky that Allah raised high. The 'its' refers to the sky.
2.grammar: A masculine noun, 'roof / vaulted height', carrying the attached possessive -hā ('its', feminine, referring to the sky). The -a vowel on the stem (samka-) is the accusative ending, marking it as the object of the verb 'raised': 'He raised its ceiling'. The pronoun -hā then shows whose ceiling — the sky's.
2.root: س-م-ك (s-m-k) — height, thickness; a raised roof or vault

3.meaning: And He shaped it and gave it balanced, well-proportioned form — completing its design with perfect symmetry. The 'it' refers back to the heaven (samā') of the previous verse.

parts.en: He made even/proportioned, fashioned in balance
it / her (object pronoun, referring to the heaven)

3.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd-person masculine singular ('He'), in the form II pattern, which intensifies the meaning to careful shaping or perfecting. Here the middle radical is the weak letter و (wāw): in form II it would normally be doubled, but because it is weak the verb surfaces as سَوَّى, ending in a long alif (a 'defective'/weak-final verb) rather than a clean sound-root pattern. The subject 'He' (Allah) is built into the verb form, not written separately. The final هَا is an attached object pronoun, 'it,' grammatically feminine because it points back to samā' (heaven). The فَ at the front links this act to the previous one in close sequence ('and then He proportioned it').
3.root: س-و-ي (s-w-y) — to be even, level, balanced, well-proportioned

1.meaning: And He made it dark — bringing on the blackness of night. Specifically used of plunging the sky/night into darkness.

parts.en: He caused (it) to grow dark, brought on darkness

1.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd-person masculine singular ('He'), in the form IV pattern, marked by the prefixed hamzatu l-qaṭʿ (the pronounced glottal hamza أَ, not a plain alif). Form IV typically carries a causative sense ('He made/caused to become dark'), but here the verb is a derived, lexicalized usage — classical Arabic uses أَغْطَشَ to mean 'to plunge into darkness / become enveloped in night's gloom,' so it is not a transparent causative of a simple form I base. The subject 'He' (Allah) is contained within the verb. The opening وَ is the connector 'and.' The object ('its night') follows as the next word.
1.root: غ-ط-ش (gh-ṭ-sh) — darkness, the falling of night's gloom

2.meaning: Its night — the period of darkness belonging to it (the heaven/sky just mentioned).
2.grammar: A noun, 'night,' carrying the -a ending here because it is the direct object of the preceding verb 'He darkened' (accusative case: it is the thing being acted upon). The attached هَا means 'its,' grammatically feminine because it refers back to the heaven (samā'). So the phrase is 'He darkened its night.'

3.meaning: And He brought out / brought forth — caused something to come out into the open. Here, He drew forth the daylight.
3.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd-person masculine singular ('He'), in the causative form IV pattern, marked by the prefixed hamzatu l-qaṭʿ (the pronounced glottal hamza أَ, not a plain alif): 'He made come out / brought forth,' as opposed to the simple form 'he went out.' The subject 'He' (Allah) is built into the verb. The opening وَ is 'and'; the thing brought out ('its morning brightness') comes next.
3.root: خ-ر-ج (kh-r-j) — going out, coming forth, emergence

4.meaning: Its morning brightness — the forenoon light, the brightness of daytime that belongs to it (the heaven). Contrasts with the 'night' just darkened.

parts.en: forenoon brightness, the full daylight of morning

4.grammar: A noun meaning the bright forenoon light. It is the direct object of the preceding verb 'He brought forth' (accusative — the thing being produced), though its final long-alif vowel does not visibly change for case. The attached هَا means 'its,' feminine, referring back to the heaven (samā'): 'and He brought forth its daylight.'
4.root: ض-ح-و (ḍ-ḥ-w) — forenoon, the brightness of full daylight

1.meaning: And the earth — introducing the earth as the next subject of Allah's creative acts.
1.grammar: The noun 'the earth' with the -a (accusative) ending, which marks it as the object of an implied or following verb ('and the earth — He spread it out'). This fronting of the object before its verb gives emphasis: 'As for the earth…' The الۡ is 'the,' and the opening وَ is 'and.'

2.meaning: After — indicating that one event followed another in time ('after that…').
2.grammar: A time-adverb meaning 'after,' always carrying the -a ending. In this verse it governs the verbal clause that follows it — بَعْدَ + دَحَاهَا — so the sense is 'after He spread it out,' i.e. 'after' here introduces an entire 'when'-clause, not just a single noun. It works like English 'after' when 'after' is followed by a whole clause ('after He did X').
2.root: ب-ع-د (b-ʿ-d) — being after, coming later, distance in time or place

3.meaning: A demonstrative pointing word meaning 'that' — referring to something distant or already mentioned. Here it points back to the preceding account of Pharaoh's fate, signalling 'that whole affair / that event'.
3.grammar: A masculine singular demonstrative for something far off, 'that (one) over there'. It is built from a pointing base (dhā) plus -li- (marking distance) plus -ka (addressing a single male listener). It is frozen in form — it does not take case endings — and here, governed by the preceding preposition fī, it serves as the topic: 'in that [there is]…'.

4.meaning: He spread it out and stretched it wide — flattening and extending the earth, making it broad and habitable. The 'it' refers to the earth.

parts.en: He spread out, stretched and leveled wide
it / her (object pronoun, referring to the earth)

4.grammar: A simple (form I) past-tense verb, 3rd-person masculine singular ('He'), with the subject 'He' (Allah) contained in the form. The final long-alif of the verb does not change for tense-mark here. The attached هَا is the object pronoun 'it,' feminine because it refers to the earth (arḍ): 'He spread it out.'
4.root: د-ح-و (d-ḥ-w) — spreading out, stretching and leveling a surface wide

1.meaning: He brought out / brought forth — caused to emerge. Here, He drew forth water and pasture from the earth.
1.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd-person masculine singular ('He'), in the causative form IV pattern, marked by the prefixed hamzatu l-qaṭʿ (the pronounced glottal hamza أَ, not a plain alif): 'He made come out / brought forth.' The subject 'He' (Allah) is built into the verb. No connector here — it opens the verse directly; the things brought forth ('its water and its pasture') follow.
1.root: خ-ر-ج (kh-r-j) — going out, coming forth, emergence

2.meaning: From it — out of it. Indicates the source from which something is drawn; here, out of the earth.

parts.en: it / her (pronoun object of the preposition)

2.grammar: The preposition مِنۡ ('from / out of') with the attached pronoun هَا ('it'). After a preposition the pronoun is in the genitive/object form. The هَا is feminine, referring back to the earth (arḍ): 'He brought forth from it [the earth]…'

3.meaning: Its water — the water belonging to it (the earth): springs, rivers, and rain-fed moisture.
3.grammar: The noun 'water' carrying the -a (accusative) ending because it is the direct object of 'He brought forth' (the thing being produced). The attached هَا means 'its,' feminine, referring to the earth: 'He brought forth from it its water.'

4.meaning: And its pasture — the grazing land and vegetation that grows for it (the earth), feeding both people and livestock.
4.grammar: A noun of place built from the root 'to graze,' meaning 'pasture / grazing land.' It is grammatically the direct object alongside 'water' (accusative — a thing brought forth), though its final long-alif does not visibly change for case. The opening وَ is 'and'; the attached هَا means 'its,' feminine, referring to the earth: 'and its pasture.'
4.root: ر-ع-ي (r-ʿ-y) — grazing, tending/pasturing livestock

1.meaning: And the mountains — the great masses of rock and earth raised up on the surface of the land.
1.grammar: A plural noun ('mountains') with the prefixed 'wa' ('and') and the definite article 'al-' ('the'). The final '-a' is the accusative ending, which marks this as the object of a verb: here it is one of the things Allah set down/made firm, so it answers 'set up WHAT?' — the mountains.

2.meaning: He fixed them firmly in place / anchored them — referring to how Allah set the mountains steady upon the earth.
2.grammar: A past-tense verb in the 'he' form: 'arsā' means 'He made (something) firm / set it as a steadfast anchor.' It comes from Form IV, which carries a causative sense ('to cause to be firm'). The attached '-hā' is the object pronoun 'them,' pointing back to the mountains. So the whole word says 'He anchored them firmly.'

1.meaning: A provision / means of enjoyment and sustenance — the benefit and support that creatures derive and live upon.
1.grammar: An indefinite noun meaning 'a provision/enjoyment.' The '-an' ending (the doubled fatḥa, called tanwīn) does two jobs: it marks the noun as indefinite ('a provision,' not 'the provision') and puts it in the accusative case. Here it functions adverbially — explaining the purpose: Allah did all this 'AS a provision' for you.

2.meaning: For you (plural) / for your benefit — addressed to a group of people.
2.grammar: A small word made of the preposition 'la-' ('for / belonging to') joined to the attached pronoun '-kum' ('you,' a group). Together they mean 'for you (all).' The '-kum' form is specifically masculine/mixed plural, addressing many people at once — the provision is for the whole community.

3.meaning: And for your grazing livestock — cattle, sheep, goats, and camels kept by people.
3.grammar: Built up from 'wa' ('and') + 'li-' ('for') + the noun 'anʿām' ('livestock') + the possessive '-kum' ('your'). The '-i' ending on the noun is genitive, which is required after the preposition 'li-' ('for'); it also links the noun to the possessor, giving 'your livestock.' Whole sense: 'and for your livestock.'

1.meaning: And then, all of a sudden — combining 'and' with a word of surprise that signals something happening abruptly and unexpectedly ('and behold, at once...').
1.grammar: Two particles, so there is no case-ending to mark. 'fa-' is a connector meaning 'and then / so', showing what follows comes next in sequence. 'idhā' here is the 'idhā of surprise' (idhā al-fujā'iyya): it dramatizes a sudden, unexpected scene — 'and all at once, there they are...'.

2.meaning: She/it comes / arrives — here, when the great event 'comes to pass.'
2.grammar: A past-tense verb, 'jāʾat,' in the feminine 'she/it' form — the '-at' ending marks a feminine subject (the calamity, which is grammatically feminine, that follows). The 'ʾ' is the hamza, the third root letter, pronounced as a glottal stop. Although past in form, after 'when' (idhā) it points to a certain future event. The final '-i' you hear is not part of the verb; it is an extra vowel added so the word flows smoothly into the next word, which begins with 'al-.'

3.meaning: The Overwhelming Calamity — a name for the Day of Resurrection, the catastrophe so immense it overwhelms and overspreads everything.
3.grammar: A noun/description with the article 'al-' ('the') from a root meaning to overflow and submerge. There are two doublings here, and they are different things. The shadda on the first 'ṭ' is NOT a root letter doubled: 'ṭ' is a sun letter, so the 'l' of 'al-' assimilates into it (you say 'aṭ-ṭ…' not 'al-ṭ…'). The genuinely doubled root consonant is the final 'm' (root ṭ-m-m), giving the intensive form 'ṭāmma,' an overwhelming feminine thing. The closing '-u' is the nominative ending, marking it as the subject — it is THE Calamity that 'comes.'

4.meaning: The greatest — the supreme, most enormous one. Here it describes the sign as the 'great(est)' sign, the most overwhelming of the miracles given to Moses.
4.grammar: A definite feminine adjective, 'the greatest,' marked by al- ('the'). It is the feminine 'elative' form (the 'biggest/greatest' pattern) agreeing with the feminine noun 'sign.' Its case ending does not change in pronunciation because it ends in the fixed long -ā; in role it is accusative, matching 'the sign' it describes ('the greatest sign').
4.root: ك-ب-ر (k-b-r) — greatness, bigness, magnitude

1.meaning: (On) the Day — pointing to a specific future Day (the Day of Resurrection). It sets the time-frame: 'the Day when…'.

parts.en: accusative ending (adverb of time: 'on the Day')

1.grammar: A noun with the '-a' ending (fatḥa, accusative). Here the accusative works as an adverb of time — 'on the Day (when)…' — and 'yawma' is also in a construct with the verb that follows ('the Day [when] it quakes'), which is why it shows the bare '-a' vowel rather than tanwīn.

2.meaning: He recalls / takes heed / brings to mind — to remember with reflection and be reminded, especially of one's own deeds.
2.grammar: A present/future-tense verb in the 'he' form: the 'ya-' prefix means 'he.' The stem is an intensive, reflexive pattern (Form V), so it means more than bare 'remember' — it is to call something to mind for oneself, to take heed and reflect. The final '-u' is the indicative ending, the normal ending for a plain statement of fact: 'he will remember / takes heed.'

3.meaning: The human being / mankind — the human person as such.
3.grammar: A noun, 'insān' ('human being'), with the article 'al-' ('the'). Used generically here, 'the human being' means humankind in general — every person. The final '-u' is the nominative ending, marking it as the subject of the verb: it is the human being who 'will remember.'

4.meaning: What / that which — here a connector meaning 'that which (he strove for).' It can also mean 'what?' as a question or 'not,' but in this verse it means 'what / that which.'
4.grammar: An unchanging little word with no case ending. In this verse it is a relative word, 'that which,' introducing the thing remembered: the human being remembers 'that which he strove for.' It does not change its form for case, gender, or number.
4.root: — (particle; no root)

5.meaning: He strove / labored / exerted effort — to work hard and pursue something with sustained effort, whether good or bad.
5.grammar: A past-tense verb in the 'he' form: 'saʿā,' 'he strove/labored.' It is one of the words whose final root letter has softened into a long 'ā' sound (written here with the dagger-alif). There is no separate ending because the 'he/it' past form carries no added suffix — the bare verb itself means 'he strove.'

1.meaning: And it was brought into full view / made plainly visible — here, the Hellfire is exposed and displayed for all to see.

parts.en: was made visible / brought out into the open

1.grammar: A past-tense passive verb with the prefixed 'wa' ('and'). The vowel pattern 'bu—rri—' (with the middle letter doubled) marks it as passive and intensive: the action is done TO the subject — it 'was brought fully into view,' not that it acted. The '-at' ending makes the subject feminine ('she/it'), agreeing with the Hellfire. The final '-i' is an extra helping vowel for smooth flow into the next word.

2.meaning: The Hellfire — the blazing fire of intense, scorching heat; one of the Qur'anic names for Hell, emphasizing its fierce flames.
2.grammar: A definite masculine noun ('the Hellfire'). The final '-u' ending marks it as the grammatical subject (nominative) — here the thing that 'will be displayed/brought into view'. The 'al-' is the definite article 'the'.
2.root: ج-ح-م (j-ḥ-m) — to blaze fiercely / intense fire

3.meaning: To / for the one who — a combination meaning 'for whoever', introducing the person for whom something is true.
3.grammar: The prefix 'li-' is a preposition meaning 'to/for'. It is attached to 'man' ('who/whoever'), a relative/conditional pronoun referring to a person. Because 'man' is built on a fixed form (indeclinable), it does not change its ending for case; the phrase as a whole means 'for the one who…'.

4.meaning: He sees / one sees — to perceive with the eyes; here, that the Hellfire is made visible 'for whoever sees', i.e. plainly in view.
4.grammar: A present/imperfect verb, 3rd person masculine singular ('he sees'). The 'ya-' prefix marks 'he' acting now/habitually. This verb has a weak final letter, so its ending appears as a long 'ā' (yarā) rather than a short vowel; in this position it is understood as indicative ('he sees'). (The doubled 'yy-' in the transliteration reflects how the previous word's article runs into it in recitation.)
4.root: ر-أ-ي (r-ʾ-y) — to see / perceive

1.meaning: Then as for… — a connecting phrase that turns to a new case or group: 'then, regarding…'. It sets up a topic and prepares for the answer that follows.
1.grammar: The prefix 'fa-' means 'then/so', linking to what came before. 'Ammā' is a detailing particle meaning 'as for…', which introduces a topic and expects a matching clause later (usually marked by 'fa-' on the answer). These are particles, so they have no case endings.

2.meaning: The one who / whoever — a pronoun pointing to a person, here 'whoever' as the subject of the condition 'whoever transgressed'.
2.grammar: A relative/conditional pronoun referring to a person ('who/whoever'). It is built on a fixed form (indeclinable), so it keeps the same shape regardless of grammatical position; here it serves as the topic introduced by 'as for…' — 'as for whoever transgressed'.

3.meaning: He transgressed / overstepped all bounds — to rebel and exceed the limits set by Allah, especially through arrogance, tyranny, and disbelief.
3.grammar: A past-tense verb, 3rd person masculine singular ('he transgressed'). The action is completed. Its final weak letter surfaces as a long 'ā' (ṭaghā); the built-in 'he' is shown by the verb form itself, with no added subject ending.

1.meaning: And he preferred / gave priority to — to choose one thing over another and favor it; here, preferring worldly life over the Hereafter.
1.grammar: The prefix 'wa-' means 'and', joining this to the previous verb. The verb is past tense, 3rd person masculine singular ('he preferred'), a Form IV (causative/transitive) pattern meaning to deliberately favor one thing over another. The final '-a' is the normal ending of such a completed verb; the 'he' is built into the form.
1.root: أ-ث-ر (ʾ-th-r) — to prefer / give precedence; a trace/mark

2.meaning: The life — living existence; here specifically the worldly life, the thing that was wrongly preferred.
2.grammar: A definite feminine noun ('the life'), object of the verb 'preferred'. The final '-a' ending marks it as the direct object (accusative) — the thing that was preferred. The 'al-' is 'the'; the feminine ending (tā' marbūṭa) is read '-ta' before its case vowel.

3.meaning: The nearer (worldly) life — 'this world', the present, lower life that is closest at hand, as opposed to the eternal Hereafter.
3.grammar: A definite feminine adjective ('the nearest/lowest'), describing 'the life' before it, so together 'the worldly life'. Literally a superlative meaning 'the nearest/lowest'. Because it ends in a fixed long 'ā', its case does not show as a short vowel; it agrees with the noun it describes (the object), so it is understood as accusative here.

1.meaning: Then indeed / so surely — a phrase that introduces an emphatic statement: 'then, most certainly…'. 'Inna' adds strong assurance, like saying 'it is truly the case that…'.
1.grammar: The prefix 'fa-' means 'then/so' and here gives the answer to the earlier 'as for…'. 'Inna' is an emphasis particle ('indeed/truly') that makes the following noun the topic and puts it in the object (accusative) case. These are particles, so they take no case ending themselves.

2.meaning: The Hellfire — the blazing fire of Hell; same fierce fire as in id 120, here named as the certain destination.
2.grammar: A definite masculine noun ('the Hellfire'). The final '-a' ending marks it as the noun governed by 'inna' (accusative) — the emphasized subject of the sentence, 'indeed the Hellfire…'. The 'al-' is 'the'.
2.root: ج-ح-م (j-ḥ-m) — to blaze fiercely / intense fire

3.meaning: 'It / she' — a standalone subject pronoun for a single feminine (or grammatically feminine) thing. Here it refers ahead to the feminine noun for the great Blast/Cry: 'it is but a single shout.'
3.grammar: An independent (standalone) subject pronoun, third-person feminine singular. It is indeclinable and takes no case ending. It functions as the subject of the sentence ('it is only...'), pointing to a feminine noun — the single mighty Blast named in the next verse.

4.meaning: The refuge / dwelling place — the final abode and shelter where one ends up and settles; here, the Hellfire as the transgressor's lasting home.
4.grammar: A definite masculine noun naming a place ('the abode/refuge') — a 'place noun' (ism makān) formed from the verb 'to take shelter'. It is the predicate, completing 'indeed the Hellfire is the refuge'. Because it ends in a fixed long 'ā', its case (nominative as predicate) does not appear as a short vowel.
4.root: أ-و-ي (ʾ-w-y) — to take shelter / give refuge

1.meaning: A two-part transition meaning 'But as for...'. It picks out one specific category and sets it apart for separate comment — here, the people who feared standing before their Lord — in pointed contrast to the opposite group mentioned just before. It signals: 'Now, turning to the case of...'

parts.en: as for / in the case of

1.grammar: Two particles joined: 'wa' (and/but) links this clause to what came before, and 'ammā' is a detailing particle that singles out a topic for separate treatment. 'Ammā' typically introduces a topic and is later answered by a clause beginning with 'fa-' ('then...'). It carries no case ending; it is a fixed function word, not a noun or verb.

2.meaning: The one who / whoever — a pronoun pointing to a person, here 'whoever' as the subject of the condition 'whoever transgressed'.
2.grammar: A relative/conditional pronoun referring to a person ('who/whoever'). It is built on a fixed form (indeclinable), so it keeps the same shape regardless of grammatical position; here it serves as the topic introduced by 'as for…' — 'as for whoever transgressed'.

3.meaning: He feared, was in awe of, dreaded. The verb covers both ordinary fear and reverent awe; in this context it is the believer's reverent dread of one day standing accountable before his Lord.
3.grammar: A past-tense (completed-action) verb, third person masculine singular: 'he feared'. The final '-a' is the standard ending of a past-tense verb in this form. The long 'ā' in the middle comes from a weak root letter (wāw) that softened into a long vowel. No subject pronoun is attached — 'he' is built into the verb form itself.

4.meaning: The act, place, or occasion of standing. Here it means 'the standing before one's Lord' — i.e. being made to stand for reckoning on the Day of Judgment, or standing in awareness of Allah's watchfulness.
4.grammar: A noun of place/occasion formed with the 'ma-' prefix, which builds nouns meaning 'the place or time of an action' from a verb. It is the direct object of 'feared', so it takes the '-a' (accusative) ending: 'he feared the standing...'. It is also in a possessive link with the following word, giving 'the standing OF his Lord' (i.e. standing before Him).
4.root: ق-و-م (q-w-m) — to stand, rise, be upright

5.meaning: His Lord — the One who creates, owns, sustains, nurtures, and has full authority over him. 'Rabb' is far richer than 'lord' or 'master': it fuses the senses of owner, sustainer, and the one who brings a thing to its completion through careful nurture.
5.grammar: A noun 'Rabb' with the attached pronoun '-hi' meaning 'his'. The '-i' ending on the noun (rabbi-) is genitive: it shows the word is possessed by the preceding noun ('the standing OF his Lord'). The pronoun is '-hi' rather than '-hu' precisely because it follows that '-i' vowel — the two harmonize. So the whole means 'of his Lord'.

6.meaning: And he held back, forbade, restrained. The verb means to keep something away from a thing it is inclined toward — here, restraining one's own soul from following its base cravings.
6.grammar: The connector 'wa' ('and') plus a past-tense verb, third person masculine singular: 'he restrained'. The verb ends in a long 'ā' written with a final weak letter (from the root's last letter yā'), which is normal for verbs whose root ends in a weak letter. 'He' is built into the form; no separate pronoun is needed.
6.root: ن-ه-ي (n-h-y) — to forbid, restrain, hold back

7.meaning: The soul, the self, the inner being — the seat of desires and appetites. In this verse it is the lower self whose cravings must be reined in.
7.grammar: The definite article 'al-' ('the') plus the noun 'nafs' ('soul'). Because 'nafs' begins with 'n' (a 'sun letter'), the 'l' of 'al-' is not pronounced; instead the 'n' is doubled (al-nafs → an-nafs). That doubled 'n' is purely a pronunciation effect — the 'n' is the first root letter of 'nafs' and belongs wholly to the noun, not to the article. The '-a' ending is accusative: 'nafs' is the direct object of 'restrained' — 'he restrained the soul'.

8.meaning: From, away from. A preposition marking separation or distance — here, holding the soul back 'from' its cravings.
8.grammar: A preposition meaning 'from / away from'.
